text: The Snowflake course's own Chapter 12 already taught you how to connect Power BI to Snowflake in general. This lesson applies that decision to Driftwood specifically -- against the real constraint this project actually has.

DirectQuery always shows the warehouse's current state, but re-runs a query on every click. Import loads a snapshot that's fast to interact with but only as fresh as its last refresh. Driftwood's requirement is a daily number, not a live one -- leadership checking at 9 AM and 4 PM should see the exact same number both times. That's Import mode's entire value proposition here.
Connecting starts the same way the Snowflake course taught: Power BI's Get Data dialog, Snowflake selected from the database connector list.
The connection dialog asks for the server and warehouse -- Driftwood points this at DRIFTWOOD_BI_WH specifically, never the ETL warehouse, so reporting never queues behind a dbt run.
Authentication connects as the DRIFTWOOD_ANALYST role -- the same read-only, marts-only role Lesson 9's RBAC work defines.

Power BI connects to exactly two tables: marts.fct_subscriptions and marts.dim_subscribers. Never raw.billing_events, never the intermediate model -- the marts are the layer dbt's tests actually run against before anything downstream sees them.

The dataset refreshes at 7 AM -- one hour after the Airflow DAG's 6 AM start, giving the full load, transform, test sequence time to finish. Refreshing at 6:05 would risk capturing the marts mid-build, showing leadership an incomplete number with no sign anything was wrong.
Next lesson: building the executive dashboard itself -- the actual MRR and churn measures leadership asked for.
